beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, it's a title; the module is about sharing what I've built.

beats.trigger: You cannot really share an agent.
beats.got: I can't hand over the agent itself. I choose between context, skill, output or interface, and that choice matters.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to something and did not use it.
beats.got: I should have brought an example. The Nordveil one is easy: the dispatch analytics portal nobody opens.

beats.trigger: **Draft** a technical plan and a people plan side by side
beats.got: A list of five verbs. The technical plan next to a people plan is the useful part.

beats.trigger: What would you want them to have: your folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: Four concrete ways to share. I can already see which of my fourteen people would want which one.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from what I built. That's fair, but it's the Jobs-to-be-Done framing I already know from consulting.

beats.trigger: The test is specificity: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent writes a JTBD file from my own material, and I check it names one person and an outcome I could observe. The page doesn't show what Claude actually wrote, so I can't tell if it was good.

beats.trigger: The four sharing strategies are:
beats.got: nothing new. This is the same four-item list as one beat ago, in nearly the same words.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: Two files are done and the next exercise builds on them.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next I name the one obstacle that matters most, then write two plans.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: I'm looking for the one cause behind many obstacles, not a list. That's a useful test for my pricing rollout.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: If my people plan has gaps next to a neat technical plan, that tells me where the rollout will fail. I like that the agent doesn't invent names.

beats.trigger: [Test the sharing plan](test-the-sharing-plan.md) checks the assumptions underneath these plans
beats.got: nothing new. It's a link to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans aren't done until someone outside the room tests them.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: I list what has to be true for them to switch. That's a sharper question than 'will they adopt it'.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: The agent writes three failure stories. The strongest one becomes a named person, a question and a test for Monday.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: A summary of what I just did. The shopping versus design line is quotable but I'd have got there without it.

beats.trigger: One law decides whether a sharing plan works.
beats.got: A lecture is coming that claims one law. Overclaiming is a Nordic red flag, so I'm sceptical.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licence counts and adoption get reported as one number, and they measure different things. I'm guilty of that in my own dashboards.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A real failure told plainly: good analysis, no decision, because leadership hadn't spent their own weeks in it. It's the CFO problem I know.

beats.trigger: They had not spent any of their own weeks inside it.
beats.got: The pricing working group won't absorb my brief unless they've worked in it. Delivering it is not enough.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily and accountability doesn't. It's neat but abstract, and I'm not sure what I'd do differently.

beats.trigger: The right choice is the one that fits the week your teammate already has.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the third time through the four strategies.

beats.trigger: So ask the question the other way round.
beats.got: nothing new. It repeats the switch question from the exercise, with examples of small, specific conditions.

beats.trigger: Send them a message today and ask for twenty minutes of their week.
beats.got: The close is one message to one person today. I can do that.

beats.got: A debrief prompt I run, and I can't see what it produces.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks, at their pace, for their reasons.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the lecture's line again.

beats.trigger: **Bring what your Monday contact said, in their own words.**
beats.got: I bring back the teammate's actual answer. That is evidence, not another plan.

beats.trigger: Module 8 puts the agent to work on the building.
beats.got: The next module is about the agent building things.

take_homes: Delivering a result is not the same as the team absorbing it. The pricing working group needs to work inside my brief, not just receive it.
Before I share anything, I ask one person what job they're trying to get done and how they do it today. Then I pick context, skill, output or interface to fit.
Put the people plan next to the technical plan. Roles with no names are where it will fail.

monday.move: Message the one pricing-working-group colleague who would use the pilot-cohort brief. Ask how they build their usage-pricing view today and what would make them stop using their spreadsheet. Then re-run the brief with fresh data and ask whether it landed where they already look.
monday.who: One named person from the pricing working group, not all fourteen of my team.
monday.stop_condition: If they say their current way is good enough and nothing would make them switch, I drop the brief as a shared thing and keep it as my own.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for context files, so whichever sharing shape I pick, the files still live in everyone's private copies.

misconception.why: The module never touches prompt writing. Its argument is that the context, the plans and the decision to switch are what matter, not the wording of any one prompt. I still think prompt quality matters inside my own work, but I no longer think it gets my team of fourteen working together.

one_line: The failure story and the 'named person, one question' ending are worth it. You get the four sharing options three times, and I couldn't see what Claude actually wrote in the exercises.
